Advanced Database models
● As the use of database systems has grown, users have demanded 
additional functionality from these software packages; 
● Increased functionality would make it easier to implement more advanced 
and complex user applications.
● The need for additional features in such applications led to the 
development of advanced database models.
● So there are active databases, deductive databases, multimedia 
databases, embedded databases, mobile databases, temporal databases 
and spatial databases and many others.

Spatial Databases-Introduction
● Spatial databases incorporate functionality that provides support for 
databases that keep track of objects in a multidimensional space. 
● For example, cartographic databases that store maps include 
two-dimensional spatial descriptions of their objects—
● from countries and states to rivers, cities, roads, seas, and so on. 
● The systems that manage geographic data and related applications are 
known as geographic information systems (GISs). 
● GIS are used in areas such as environmental applications, transportation 
systems, emergency response systems, and battle management. 
● Other databases, such as meteorological databases for weather 
information, are three-dimensional.

Different kinds of spatial analyses
● Spatial analysis operations, which often use statistical techniques, are used to 
uncover spatial relationships within and among mapped data layers.
● Flow analysis operations help in determining the shortest path between two points 
and also the connectivity among nodes or regions in a graph. 
● Location analysis aims to find if the given set of points and lines lie within a given 
polygon (location).
● Digital terrain analysis is used to build three-dimensional models, where the 
topography of a geographical location can be represented with an x, y, z data 
model known as Digital Terrain (or Elevation) Model (DTM/DEM).
● Spatial search allows a user to search for objects within a particular spatial region.
● There are also topological relationships among spatial objects.

Spatial Data Types
● Map data includes various geographic or spatial features of objects in a map, such as 
an object’s shape and the location of the object within the map.
● The three basic types of features are points, lines, and polygons (or areas).
● Points are used to represent spatial characteristics of objects whose locations 
correspond to a single 2-D coordinate (x, y, or longitude/latitude) in the scale of a 
particular application. 
● Some examples of point objects could be buildings, cellular towers, or stationary 
vehicles.
● Moving vehicles and other moving objects can be represented by a sequence of point 
locations that change over time. 
● Lines represent objects having length, such as roads or rivers, whose spatial 
characteristics can be approximated by a sequence of connected lines. 
● Polygons are used to represent spatial characteristics of objects that have a boundary, 
such as countries, states, lakes, or cities.

stored in the bucket.

space so that each point belongs to precisely one bucket.

○ Similar to B+-tree indexes in traditional database systems.

○ Spatial join indexes, can be used to speed up spatial join operations.
2. The two-dimensional (2-D) spatial data is converted to single-dimensional

○ so that traditional indexing techniques (B+-tree) can be used.

Spatial Data Indexing
Grid Files
● A grid file is a multi-dimensional data structure used to handle indexing 
and efficient querying across two or more search keys simultaneously.
● It acts as a symmetric multi-key indexing scheme.
● Records are visualized as points in an n-dimensional space. 
○ where each dimension represents the domain of a specific attribute.
○ e.g., latitude, longitude, or age and salary.
● The search space is split into a grid using linear scales along each axis.
● The actual data records are grouped and stored in data buckets on the 
disk. 
● Multiple grid cells (regions of the multi-dimensional space) can point to 
the same bucket if they share space or if data density is low.

Spatial Data Indexing
Grid Files
● They can also be used for indexing n-dimensional spatial data. 
● The fixed-grid method divides an n-dimensional hyperspace into equal 
size buckets. 
● The data structure that implements the fixed grid is an n-dimensional 
array. 
● The objects whose spatial locations lie within a cell (totally or partially) can 
be stored in a dynamic structure to handle overflows.
● Useful for uniformly distributed data like satellite imagery.
● The fixed-grid structure is rigid, and its directory can be sparse and large.

R-trees
● A height-balanced tree.
● An extension of the B+-tree for k-dimensions, where k > 1.
● Designed for spatial data storage and multi-dimensional indexing.
● spatial objects are approximated in the R-tree by their minimum 
bounding rectangle (MBR).
● MBR is the smallest rectangle, with sides parallel to the coordinate system 
(x and y) axis, that contains the object.

Spatial Data Indexing
R-trees: Properties
● Consists of a single root, internals nodes, and leaf nodes.
● The root contains the pointer to the largest region in the spatial domain.
● Parent nodes contains pointers to their child nodes where the region of 
child nodes completely overlaps the regions of parent nodes.
● Leaf nodes contains data about the MBR to the current objects.
● MBR-Minimum bounding region refers to the minimal bounding box 
parameter surrounding the region/object under consideration.

Quad-trees
● A tree data structure.
● used to partition a two-dimensional space into smaller regions.
● each node in the tree has four children, corresponding to the four 
quadrants of the space.
● useful for spatial indexing and searching.
● It allows efficient insertion, deletion, and retrieval of objects based on 
their spatial location.
● It can efficiently handle spatial queries such as range searches and 
nearest neighbor searches.
● Applications: GIS, computer graphics, video games, image processing.

Spatial Data Indexing
Quad-trees
● The quadtree starts with a root node that represents the entire space. 
● Each level of the tree divides the space into four equal-sized quadrants. 
● Each node of a Quad Tree has at most four children.
● The leaf nodes of the tree represent smaller regions of the space.

slides.text:
Spatial Data Indexing
Quad-trees: Construction
1. Divide the current two-dimensional space into four boxes.
2. If a box contains one or more points in it, create a child object, storing in it 
the two-dimensional space of the box.
3. If a box does not contain any points, do not create a child for it.
4. Recurse for each of the children.

Mobile Computing Architecture
● A distributed architecture where a number of computers, generally 
referred to as Fixed Hosts and Base Stations, are interconnected through 
a high-speed wired network. 
● Fixed hosts are general purpose computers that are not typically 
equipped to manage mobile units but can be configured to do so. 
● Base stations function as gateways to the fixed network for the Mobile 
Units. 
● They are equipped with wireless interfaces and offer network access 
services of which mobile units are clients.

Mobile Computing Architecture
Layers of Architecture:
1. Mobile Device Layer – hardware, OS, local DB (e.g., SQLite)
2. Network Layer – wireless communication, protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP, 
MQTT)
3. Middleware Layer – synchronization, caching, security services
4. Server/Cloud Layer – enterprise DBMS, application servers, APIs

physically separate or detached from the corporate database server but 
has the capability to communicate with those servers from remote sites 
allowing the sharing of various kinds of data.
● Mobile databases are databases designed to operate on mobile devices 
or in mobile environments, enabling data access, synchronization, and 
management anytime, anywhere.

laptop, PDA, or other Internet access device that is required for 
applications at remote sites.

Characteristics of Mobile Environments
● Portability
● Lower bandwidth
● Range, interference
● Locality of access 
● Support for packet switching
● High communication latency
● Limited storage & processing power
● Frequent disconnections
● Synchronization with central servers
● Security & privacy concerns

Data Management Issues
● Connectivity Issues
○ Frequent disconnections, variable bandwidth
● Consistency & Synchronization
○ Conflict resolution in replicated data
● Resource Constraints
○ Limited CPU, memory, battery
● Security & Privacy
○ Protecting sensitive data on mobile devices
● Scalability
○ Handling millions of concurrent mobile users
● Data Distribution
○ Managing data across heterogeneous devices and networks

Data Synchronization
● Why synchronization is needed?
● Techniques:
○ Two-way sync
○ Conflict detection & resolution
○ Replication strategies

Query Processing in Mobile Databases
● Constraints: low bandwidth, limited CPU
● Query optimization for mobile
● Use of caching and indexing
● Example: location-based queries in ride-hailing apps

Security in Mobile Databases
● Threats: unauthorized access, data leakage
● Techniques:
○ Authentication & authorization
○ Encryption (at rest & in transit)
○ Secure APIs
● Example: Mobile banking apps

Types of Mobile Databases
● Local Databases (SQLite, Realm)
● Remote Databases (Firebase, AWS DynamoDB)
● Hybrid Approaches (offline-first with sync)
● Examples in real-world apps

Popular Mobile Database Systems
● SQLite – lightweight, embedded
● Realm – object-oriented, offline-first
● Firebase Realtime Database – cloud-hosted, sync across clients
● Couchbase Mobile – NoSQL, sync with Couchbase Server
